name: Gentamicin
route_note: IV or IM, typically as once-daily extended-interval dosing with level monitoring; also eye/ear drops and topical cream.
targets: 16S rRNA of the 30S ribosomal subunit (A site)

discovery.by: Marvin Weinstein, Gerald Wagman and George Luedemann (Schering Corporation)
discovery.note: Isolated from the actinomycete Micromonospora purpurea; the '-micin' spelling reflects its Micromonospora origin.

tagline: Inexpensive aminoglycoside for Gram-negative sepsis and synergy in endocarditis
summary: Gentamicin is an aminoglycoside antibiotic produced by Micromonospora purpurea and discovered at Schering in 1963. It is rapidly bactericidal against aerobic Gram-negative bacteria and widely used for sepsis, neonatal infections and, in combination, for some Gram-positive endocarditis, with toxicity limiting its use.
mechanism: Aminoglycosides are polycationic molecules that cross the Gram-negative outer membrane by self-promoted uptake and enter the cytoplasm by an oxygen-dependent transport process, which is why they are inactive against anaerobes. Inside, they bind the decoding A site of 16S rRNA in the 30S subunit, causing misreading of mRNA and production of aberrant proteins that damage the membrane, accelerating uptake; killing is rapid and concentration-dependent.

Against streptococci and enterococci it acts synergistically with cell-wall-active agents such as ampicillin, which increase its uptake. Resistance is mostly due to aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes (acetyltransferases, phosphotransferases, nucleotidyltransferases) and 16S rRNA methyltransferases.
uses: Gram-negative sepsis, pyelonephritis and complicated urinary infections
Synergistic therapy of streptococcal and enterococcal endocarditis

history.title: Discovery
history.detail: Schering scientists report gentamicin from Micromonospora purpurea.

history.title: Clinical introduction
history.detail: Gentamicin enters clinical use in the mid-1960s and becomes a mainstay against Pseudomonas and Enterobacterales.

history.title: Mitochondrial deafness gene
history.detail: The mitochondrial MT-RNR1 m.1555A>G variant is identified as a cause of aminoglycoside-induced deafness.

history.title: Once-daily dosing
history.detail: Extended-interval (once-daily) aminoglycoside dosing is widely adopted after studies show equal efficacy with less toxicity.

history.title: Point-of-care genetic test
history.detail: NICE recommends rapid MT-RNR1 genotyping for babies who may need gentamicin in neonatal intensive care.

pk.half_life: about 2–3 hours with normal renal function (much longer in neonates and renal impairment)

safety.boxed_warning: US labels warn of potential nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity and neurotoxicity; monitor serum concentrations and renal function and avoid other nephrotoxic or ototoxic drugs.

facts: People carrying the MT-RNR1 m.1555A>G variant can become permanently deaf after a single aminoglycoside dose.
Gentamicin is a mixture of related components (C1, C1a, C2, C2a).
